claim: S3 Standard storage is designed for 99.999999999% durability and 99.99% availability of objects over a given year, and the multi-zone classes store objects on multiple devices across a minimum of three Availability Zones in a Region.
question: What durability and availability is S3 Standard designed for, over what period, and across how many Availability Zones?

evidence.quote: Designed to provide 99.999999999% durability and 99.99% availability of objects over a given year.

S3 Standard, S3 Intelligent-Tiering, S3 Standard-IA, S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and S3 Glacier Deep Archive redundantly store objects on multiple devices across a minimum of three Availability Zones in an AWS Region.

claim: Every storage class except S3 One Zone-IA and S3 Express One Zone is designed to survive the physical loss of an entire Availability Zone.
question: Which S3 storage classes are not designed to survive the loss of an Availability Zone?

values.spoken: all classes except One Zone-IA and Express One Zone

evidence.quote: Be aware that all of the storage classes except for S3 One Zone-IA (`ONEZONE_IA`) and S3 Express One Zone (`EXPRESS_ONEZONE`) are designed to be resilient to the physical loss of an Availability Zone resulting from disasters.

S3 Standard, S3 Intelligent-Tiering, S3 Standard-IA, S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and S3 Glacier Deep Archive are all designed to sustain data in the event of the loss of an entire Amazon S3 Availability Zone.

claim: By default an object is stored in the S3 Standard storage class; if you do not specify a class at upload, S3 assigns S3 Standard.
question: Which storage class does an object get when none is specified?

qualifiers.condition: no storage class given at upload

evidence.quote: By default, objects in S3 are stored in the S3 Standard storage class, however Amazon S3 offers a range of other storage classes for the objects that you store.
If you don't specify the storage class when you upload an object, Amazon S3 assigns the S3 Standard storage class.

claim: S3 Express One Zone delivers consistent single-digit millisecond data access, up to 10x faster than S3 Standard with request costs 50 percent lower, and stores data redundantly on multiple devices within a single Availability Zone.
question: What latency does S3 Express One Zone give, how does it compare to S3 Standard, and where is the data stored?

qualifiers.scope: S3 Express One Zone storage class

evidence.quote: **S3 Express One Zone** (`EXPRESS_ONEZONE`) – Amazon S3 Express One Zone is a high-performance, single-zone Amazon S3 storage class that is purpose-built to deliver consistent, single-digit millisecond data access for your most latency-sensitive applications. S3 Express One Zone is the lowest latency cloud object storage class available today, with data access speed up to 10x faster and with request costs 50 percent lower than S3 Standard. With S3 Express One Zone, your data is redundantly stored on multiple devices within a single Availability Zone.

note: The S3 FAQ says request costs up to 80% lower than S3 Standard; the user guide says 50 percent. The guide figure is kept here; the FAQ lens records the other.

claim: S3 One Zone-IA stores data in only one Availability Zone, is as durable as S3 Standard-IA but less available, and is not resilient to the physical loss of that Availability Zone; use it for data you can re-create, such as CRR replicas.
question: What does S3 One Zone-IA give up compared with S3 Standard-IA, and what data is it meant for?

values.display: not resilient to the physical loss of the Availability Zone
values.spoken: not resilient to the loss of its Availability Zone

values.display: re-create the data if the Availability Zone fails

evidence.quote: However, the data is not resilient to the physical loss of the Availability Zone resulting from disasters, such as earthquakes and floods. The S3 One Zone-IA storage class is as durable as S3 Standard-IA, but it is less available and less resilient.
**S3 One Zone-IA** (`ONEZONE_IA`) – Use if you can re-create the data if the Availability Zone fails, for object replicas when configuring S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR).

claim: AWS recommends S3 Standard-IA for the primary or only copy of data that cannot be re-created; its objects are resilient to the loss of an Availability Zone.
question: When should S3 Standard-IA be chosen over S3 One Zone-IA?

values.display: primary or only copy of data that can't be re-created
values.spoken: the only copy of data you cannot re-create

evidence.quote: **S3 Standard-IA** (`STANDARD_IA`) – Use for your primary or only copy of data that can't be re-created.
S3 Standard-IA objects are resilient to the loss of an Availability Zone. This storage class offers greater availability and resiliency than the S3 One Zone-IA class.

claim: S3 Standard-IA and S3 One Zone-IA have a 30-day minimum storage duration: an object deleted, overwritten or transitioned before 30 days is charged the normal storage charge plus a pro-rated charge for the rest of the 30 days.
question: What happens to the bill when an S3 Standard-IA or One Zone-IA object is deleted before 30 days?

values.display: pro-rated charge for the remainder of the 30-day minimum
values.spoken: a pro-rated charge for the rest of the thirty days

qualifiers.scope: per object in S3 Standard-IA or S3 One Zone-IA
qualifiers.condition: object deleted, overwritten or transitioned before 30 days

evidence.quote: If you delete an object before the end of the 30-day minimum storage duration period, you are charged for 30 days. Objects that are deleted, overwritten, or transitioned to a different storage class before 30 days will incur the normal storage usage charge plus a pro-rated charge for the remainder of the 30-day minimum.

claim: S3 Standard-IA and S3 One Zone-IA bill a minimum of 128 KB per object: an object smaller than 128 KB is charged as 128 KB, so these classes suit objects larger than 128 KB kept for at least 30 days.
question: What is the minimum billable object size in S3 Standard-IA and S3 One Zone-IA?

qualifiers.scope: per object in S3 Standard-IA or S3 One Zone-IA

evidence.quote: The S3 Standard-IA and S3 One Zone-IA storage classes are suitable for objects larger than 128 KB that you plan to store for at least 30 days. If an object is less than 128 KB, Amazon S3 charges you for 128 KB.

claim: Each object archived to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive carries 40 KB of extra metadata: 8 KB billed at S3 Standard rates (name and metadata, so the object still lists in real time) and 32 KB billed at the Glacier class rate (index data needed to restore it).
question: How much per-object overhead is billed for objects in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive, and at what rates?

qualifiers.scope: per object archived to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive

evidence.quote: The minimum storage duration charges (90 days for S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, 180 days for S3 Glacier Deep Archive) and the per-object storage overhead (40 KB total, of which 8 KB is charged at S3 Standard rates and 32 KB at the destination Glacier rate) also begin at this point.

For each object archived to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive, Amazon S3 uses 8 KB of storage for the name of the object and other metadata. Amazon S3 stores this metadata so that you can get a real-time list of your archived objects by using the Amazon S3 API.

For each object that is archived to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive, Amazon S3 adds 32 KB of storage for index and related metadata. This extra data is necessary to identify and restore your object. You are charged S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive rates for this additional storage.

claim: The minimum storage duration is 90 days for S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and 180 days for S3 Glacier Deep Archive; deleting or overwriting an archived object inside that period costs a prorated early deletion fee.
question: What are the minimum storage durations of S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive, and what does an early delete cost?

qualifiers.scope: per object in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive

evidence.quote: The minimal storage duration period is 90 days for the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class and 180 days for S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
If you delete or overwrite an archived object within the minimal duration period, Amazon S3 charges a prorated early deletion fee.

claim: Since September 2024 a Lifecycle configuration by default does not transition objects smaller than 128 KB to any storage class, because each transition is a billed request; an object size filter in the rule allows them. Before September 2024 such objects could by default transition only to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
question: Does a Lifecycle rule transition objects smaller than 128 KB by default?

values.display: prevents objects smaller than 128 KB from being transitioned to any storage class
values.spoken: objects under one twenty-eight kilobytes are not transitioned

qualifiers.condition: ObjectSizeGreaterThan or ObjectSizeLessThan filter, or the x-amz-transition-default-minimum-object-size header, changes it

evidence.quote: Amazon S3 applies a default behavior to S3 Lifecycle configurations that prevents objects smaller than 128 KB from being transitioned to any storage class. We don't recommend transitioning objects less than 128 KB because you are charged a transition request for each object.

**Previous default transition behavior** — Before September 2024, the default behavior allowed objects smaller than 128 KB to be transitioned only to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage classes.
**Updated default transition behavior** — Starting September 2024, the default behavior prevents objects smaller than 128 KB from being transitioned to any storage class.

changed.was: allowed objects smaller than 128 KB to be transitioned only to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage classes

claim: A single Lifecycle rule cannot transition an object to a second storage class before the first class's minimum storage duration has passed: after S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (90 days minimum) at day 4, the Deep Archive transition must be at day 94 or later.
question: Can one Lifecycle rule move an object to Glacier Instant Retrieval at day 4 and to Deep Archive at day 20?

values.display: before the minimum storage duration period has passed
values.spoken: not before the minimum storage duration has passed

qualifiers.condition: two rules can do it, but the minimum duration charges still apply

evidence.quote: You can't create a single Lifecycle rule that transitions objects from one storage class to another before the minimum storage duration period has passed.

For example, S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval has a minimum storage duration of 90 days. You can't specify a lifecycle rule that transitions objects to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 4 days, and then transitions objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 20 days. In this case the S3 Glacier Deep Archive transition must occur after at least 94 days.
You can specify two rules to accomplish this, but you pay the minimum duration storage charges.

claim: Transitioning an object out of a storage class before that class's minimum storage duration is billed for the remainder of the duration.
question: What does a Lifecycle transition cost when it moves an object before its minimum storage duration ends?

values.display: charged for the remainder of that duration
values.spoken: charged for the rest of the minimum duration

qualifiers.condition: the source class has a minimum storage duration

evidence.quote: Certain storage classes have a minimum object storage duration. If you transition objects out of these storage classes before the minimum duration, you are charged for the remainder of that duration.

claim: Lifecycle transitions to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive run asynchronously, but billing at the destination class rate, its minimum duration and its per-object overhead start on the date the rule is satisfied, even before the physical move; only transitions to S3 Intelligent-Tiering bill after the physical transition completes.
question: When does billing switch to the Glacier rate after a Lifecycle transition rule matches an object?

values.display: starting from the date the lifecycle rule is satisfied
values.spoken: from the date the rule is satisfied

qualifiers.condition: destination S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive

evidence.quote: You are charged at the destination storage class rate (S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive) starting from the date the lifecycle rule is satisfied, even if the physical transition has not yet occurred.
The only exception is transitions to S3 Intelligent-Tiering, where billing changes occur after the physical transition completes.

claim: A Lifecycle rule can move an S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval object only to S3 Glacier Deep Archive, and nothing moves out of S3 Glacier Deep Archive by Lifecycle; to change class you restore a temporary copy and then copy the object into the new class.
question: Can a Lifecycle rule move an object from a Glacier class back to S3 Standard?

evidence.quote: The transition of objects to the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class can go only one way.

You cannot use an S3 Lifecycle configuration rule to convert the storage class of an object from S3 Glacier Deep Archive to any other storage class. If you want to change the storage class of an archived object to another storage class, you must use the restore operation to make a temporary copy of the object first.
Objects that are stored in the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class can only be transitioned to the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class.

claim: An archived object in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive is not readable in real time: you restore a temporary copy for a number of days you choose, and during that time you pay for both the archive and the temporary copy at the S3 Standard rate while the object's storage class stays the Glacier class.
question: What does a restore from S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive produce, and what is billed meanwhile?

values.spoken: you pay for both the archive and the copy

evidence.quote: Archived objects are Amazon S3 objects, but before you can access an archived object, you must first restore a temporary copy of it. The restored object copy is available only for the duration that you specify in the restore request. After that, Amazon S3 deletes the temporary copy, and the object remains archived in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
When you restore an archive, you are paying for both the archive (S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive rate) and a copy that you restored temporarily (S3 Standard storage rate).
After you receive a temporary copy of the restored object, the object's storage class remains S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

claim: S3 processes only one restore request at a time per object.
question: How many restore requests can be in progress for one archived object?

values.display: only one restore request at a time per object
values.spoken: one restore at a time per object

evidence.quote: Amazon S3 processes only one restore request at a time per object.

claim: S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves an object to the Infrequent Access tier after 30 consecutive days without access and to the Archive Instant Access tier after 90 days without access, for a small monthly monitoring and automation charge and with no performance impact.
question: After how many days without access does S3 Intelligent-Tiering move an object to the Infrequent Access and Archive Instant Access tiers?

evidence.quote: For a low monthly object monitoring and automation charge, S3 Intelligent-Tiering monitors access patterns and automatically moves objects to the Infrequent Access tier when they haven't been accessed for 30 consecutive days. After 90 days of no access, the objects are moved to the Archive Instant Access tier without performance impact or operational overhead.

claim: When an object in the Infrequent Access or Archive Instant Access tier is accessed again, S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves it back to the Frequent Access tier automatically; a GetObject, PutObject or CopyObject counts as access, a HeadObject or ListObjects does not.
question: What happens when an object in an Intelligent-Tiering lower tier is read again, and which requests count as access?

values.display: automatically moved back to the Frequent Access tier
values.spoken: moved back to the Frequent Access tier

evidence.quote: If an object in the Infrequent Access tier or Archive Instant Access tier is accessed later, it is automatically moved back to the Frequent Access tier.
Other actions **don't** constitute access that automatically moves objects from the Infrequent Access tier or the Archive Instant Access tier back to the Frequent Access tier.

claim: The optional Archive Access tier archives objects not accessed for a minimum of 90 consecutive days and the optional Deep Archive Access tier after a minimum of 180 consecutive days; for both, the number of days can be set up to a maximum of 730 days, and objects in them must be restored with RestoreObject before they can be read.
question: What are the optional Intelligent-Tiering archive tiers, after how many days do they activate, and how is an archived object read?

values.spoken: at least one hundred eighty consecutive days
up to seven hundred thirty days

qualifiers.condition: the archive tiers are opt-in; last-access threshold configurable between the minimum and 730 days

evidence.quote: With Archive Access, S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves objects that have not been accessed for a minimum of 90 consecutive days to the Archive Access tier. With Deep Archive Access, S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves objects to the Deep Archive Access tier after a minimum of 180 consecutive days of no access. For both tiers, you can configure the number of days of no access based on your needs.
You can extend the last access time for archiving to a maximum of 730 days.
If the object that you are retrieving is stored in the Archive Access or Deep Archive Access tiers, you must first restore the object by using the `RestoreObject` operation.

claim: A Standard retrieval from the Intelligent-Tiering Archive Access tier takes 3–5 hours and from the Deep Archive Access tier occurs within 12 hours; the tiers perform like S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive, and the Archive Instant Access tier keeps millisecond access.
question: How long does a restore from the Intelligent-Tiering Archive Access and Deep Archive Access tiers take?

qualifiers.scope: per object in the S3 Intelligent-Tiering archive tiers

evidence.quote: Standard retrieval times for this access tier can range from 3–5 hours. If you initiate your restore request by using S3 Batch Operations, your restore starts within minutes.
Standard retrieval of objects in this access tier occurs within 12 hours. If you initiate your restore request by using S3 Batch Operations, your restore starts within 9 hours.
The Archive Access tier delivers slightly lower storage costs, with minute-to-hour retrieval times. The Archive Instant Access tier delivers millisecond access and high-throughput performance.

claim: An object smaller than 128 KB in S3 Intelligent-Tiering is not monitored and not eligible for automatic tiering: it always stays in the Frequent Access tier, is billed at Frequent Access rates and does not incur the monitoring and automation charge.
question: Are objects smaller than 128 KB auto-tiered in S3 Intelligent-Tiering, and how are they billed?

values.display: always stored in the Frequent Access tier
values.spoken: always kept in the Frequent Access tier

evidence.quote: If the size of an object is less than 128 KB, it is not monitored and is not eligible for automatic tiering. Smaller objects are always stored in the Frequent Access tier.

S3 Intelligent-Tiering has no minimum eligible object size, but objects smaller than 128 KB are not eligible for auto tiering. These smaller objects may be stored, but they’ll always be charged at the Frequent Access tier rates and don’t incur the monitoring and automation charge.

claim: S3 Intelligent-Tiering has no retrieval fees and no minimum storage duration, and is designed for 99.9% availability and 99.999999999% durability.

evidence.quote: There are no retrieval fees for S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
S3 Intelligent-Tiering is designed for 99.9% availability and 99.999999999% durability.
No operational overhead, no lifecycle charges, no retrieval charges, and no minimum storage duration

claim: AWS states storage savings of 40% in the Infrequent Access tier, 68% in the Archive Instant Access tier, and up to 95% in the Deep Archive Access tier, compared with the Frequent Access tier.
